Surah Al 'Imran

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ ﴿He has sent down upon you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it, and He revealed the Torah and the Gospel﴾ ﴿before, as guidance for mankind, and He sent down the Criterion. Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah will have a severe punishment, and Allah is Exalted in Might, Owner of Retribution﴾

﴿Alif, Lam, Mim﴾ ﴿Allah, there is no deity except Him, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence﴾ We have already mentioned the interpretation of this before.

If it is said: "Alif, Lam, Mim" is one of the names of Allah, the Exalted, then His saying "Allah, there is no deity except Him" is an epithet of the one named by it, and its explanation is that Alif, Lam, Mim is Allah, there is no deity except Him.

If it is said: it is an oath, then it falls upon the statement that He, glory be to Him, is the one deity besides whom there is no deity, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence, affirming His being God and negating that anyone else be God.

If it is said according to other interpretations besides these two, then what follows is a described subject, and that Allah is the One besides whom there is no deity, the Ever-Living, the Sustainer of existence.

This verse, along with nearly eighty-some verses of the surah, was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran from the Christians, when they came to dispute with the Prophet ﷺ; they were fourteen men of their nobles.

﴿He has sent down upon you the Book in truth﴾ Regarding this there are two views. One: with justice, in what He made incumbent upon you of the burdens of prophethood. (p-368)

The second: with justice regarding what He singled you out with of the honour of messengership.

And if it is said that it means truthfulness, then there are two views. One: with truthfulness in what it contains of reports about past generations and earlier nations.

The second: with truthfulness in what it contains of the promise of reward for obedience to Him, and the warning of punishment for disobedience to Him.

﴿Confirming what was before it﴾ That is, the book and messenger that came before it. It was said that what came before it is "before it" because it is manifest to it, just as what is before a thing is manifest.

Regarding His saying ﴿confirming what was before it﴾ there are two views. One: its meaning is informing about what came before it, with the truthful report that indicates its miraculous nature.

The second: its meaning is that it informs of the truthfulness of the prophets in what they brought, unlike those who believe in some and disbelieve in others.

His saying, mighty and majestic: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah﴾ Regarding this there are two views. One: by His proofs and arguments.

The second: by the signs of the Qur'an. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means the delegation of Najran when they came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to dispute with him.

﴿will have a severe punishment﴾ meaning the punishment of Hell.

﴿And Allah is Exalted in Might﴾ Regarding this there are two views. One: in His refusal (to be overcome).

The second: in His power.

﴿Owner of Retribution﴾ Regarding this there are two views. One: Owner of might and force.

The second: Owner of exacting (requital).

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on Surah 3, verses 5–9:**

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿It is He who has sent down to you the Book﴾, meaning the Qur'an.

﴿Among it are verses that are decisive (muhkamat), they are the foundation of the Book, and others that are ambiguous (mutashabihat)﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) differed over its interpretation (ta'wil) in seven opinions:

The first: the *muhkam* is the abrogating (nasikh) and the *mutashabih* is the abrogated (mansukh). This was said by Ibn Abbas and Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: the *muhkam* is that whose lawful and unlawful rulings Allah has made clear, so its meanings are not confused. This was said by Mujahid.

The third: the *muhkam* is that which admits of only one interpretation, and the *mutashabih* is that which admits of several. This was said by al-Shafi'i and Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr.

The fourth: the *muhkam* is that whose wording is not repeated, and the *mutashabih* is that whose wording is repeated. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: the *muhkam* is the obligations (fara'id), the promise and the threat (wa'd and wa'id), and the *mutashabih* is the narratives (qasas) and the parables (amthal).

The sixth: the *muhkam* is that whose interpretation and meaning and explanation (tafsir) the scholars know, and the *mutashabih* is that for which there is no way to knowledge of it, being among what Allah has reserved for His own knowledge, such as the Hour (qiyamah), the rising of the sun from its west, the descent of Jesus, and the like. This is the saying of Jabir ibn Abd Allah.

The seventh: the *muhkam* is that which stands by itself and does not need inference (istidlal).

It may also admit an eighth opinion: the *muhkam* is that whose rulings have intelligible meanings, and the *mutashabih* is that whose rulings have unintelligible meanings, such as the number of the prayers and the restriction of fasting to the month of Ramadan rather than Sha'ban.

He made it *muhkam* and *mutashabih* only to call for reflection (istidh'a' lil-nazar), without relying solely on report. Mu'adh ibn Jabal narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The Qur'an is in three parts: the lawful, so follow it; the unlawful, so avoid it; and the ambiguous, which is unclear to you, so refer it to its knower."

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿they are the foundation of the Book﴾, there are two interpretations. The first: the origin of the Book. The second: the known (ma'lum) of the Book.

Within this there are two explanations. The first: that He meant the verses in which the obligations and the limits (hudud) are found. This was said by Yahya ibn Ya'mur.

The second: that He meant the opening letters of the surahs, from which the Qur'an is derived. This is the saying of Abu Fakhitah.

It may also admit a third meaning: that He intends by it that it is intelligible in its meanings, because what shares its meaning branches off from it, so the root becomes for its branches like the mother (umm) for what comes into being from her. For this reason He named it "the mother of the Book."

﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation (zaygh)﴾: there are two explanations. The first: inclination away from the truth. The second: doubt. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿they follow what is ambiguous of it﴾: there are three explanations. The first: it is the term (ajal) that the Jews wished to know from the disjointed letters (al-huruf al-muqatta'ah), by the reckoning of the abjad (hisab al-jummal), of the end of the period of the Prophet (ﷺ). The second: it is knowledge of the outcomes of the Qur'an, through knowing in advance the occurrence of abrogation before its time. The third: that this was revealed concerning the delegation of Najran when they disputed with the Prophet (ﷺ) about the Messiah. They said: "Is he not the Word of Allah and His Spirit?" He said: "Yes." They said: "That is enough for us." So Allah, exalted, revealed: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is deviation, they follow what is ambiguous of it, seeking discord and seeking its interpretation﴾. This is the saying of al-Rabi'.

Regarding His saying, exalted is He, ﴿seeking discord (fitnah)﴾, there are four explanations. The first: polytheism (shirk), said by al-Suddi. The second: confusion (labs), said by Mujahid. The third: the doubts with which they disputed with the delegation of Najran. The fourth: the sowing of discord among people (ifsad dhat al-bayn).

﴿and seeking its interpretation (ta'wil)﴾: regarding ta'wil there are two explanations. The first: that it is tafsir. The second: that it is the awaited outcome (al-aqibah al-muntazarah).

﴿And none knows its interpretation except Allah﴾: regarding this there are three opinions. The first: the interpretation of the whole of the *mutashabih* is known only to Allah, because among it is what people know and among it is what none knows but Allah. This was said by al-Hasan.

The second: its interpretation is on the Day of Resurrection, because of what it contains of promise and threat, as Allah, exalted, said: ﴿Do they await anything but its fulfilment? On the day its fulfilment comes﴾ [al-A'raf: 53], meaning the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The third: its interpretation is the time of its occurrence. This was said by some of the later scholars.

﴿And those firmly grounded in knowledge (al-rasikhun fi al-'ilm)﴾: there are two explanations. The first: that means those steadfast in it, who act upon it. The second: that means those who derive knowledge (al-mustanbitun li-l-'ilm) and act upon it. Concerning them there are two explanations. The first: that they are included in the exception, and the meaning is: "The one who knows its interpretation is Allah and those firmly grounded in knowledge, all together."

Ibn Abi Najih narrated from Ibn Abbas that he said: "I am among those who know its interpretation."

The second: that they are excluded from the exception, and the meaning of the statement is: "None knows its interpretation except Allah alone." Then He began anew, saying: ﴿and those firmly grounded in knowledge say: "We believe in it; all of it is from our Lord."﴾ This admits two meanings. The first: the knowledge of that is with our Lord. The second: what He distinguished of the *muhkam* and the *mutashabih* came down from our Lord.

Al-Mawardi, Commentary (al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun) on Surah 3, verses 10–11:

His words, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Like the habit of the people of Pharaoh﴾. There are two interpretations concerning this. The first: al-da'b (دَأْب) means habit, i.e., like the habit of the people of Pharaoh and those before them.

The second: al-da'b here means diligence (al-ijtihad), derived from their saying, "da'abtu fi al-amr" (دَأبْتُ في الأمْرِ), when one exerts oneself in the matter.

If it is said that it means habit, then regarding what it points to of their habit there are two interpretations. The first: like their habit of denying the truth. The second: like their habit of punishing them for their sins.

And if it is said that it means diligence, then what it points to of their diligence may carry two interpretations. The first: like their diligence in supporting disbelief over faith. The second: like their diligence in denial and false slander.

Concerning those to whom it refers, that they are "like the people of Pharaoh," there are two opinions. The first: they are the polytheists of Quraysh on the day of Badr, who were, in God's retribution against them for His messengers and the believers, like the people of Pharaoh in His retribution against them for Moses and the Children of Israel. Accordingly, on the first opinion this is a reminder to the Messenger and the believers of a blessing that had already preceded, since this verse was revealed after Badr, calling for their gratitude for it. On the second opinion, it is a promise of a future blessing, since it was revealed before the killing of the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa', so He fulfilled His promise and made it a miracle for His Messenger.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 12–13:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: "You will be overcome"﴾ — the verse.

Regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse there are three opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the Quraysh a year before Badr. So Allah fulfilled His word, confirmed His Messenger, and carried out His promise regarding those among them who were killed on the Day of Badr. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.

The second: it was revealed concerning the Banu Qaynuqa, when the Quraysh were destroyed on the Day of Badr. The Prophet (ﷺ) invited them to Islam and warned them of what had befallen the Quraysh. They refused and said: "We are not like the Quraysh, the inexperienced ones who do not know people." So Allah revealed this verse concerning them. This was said by Qatadah and Ibn Ishaq.

The third: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers in general.

Regarding "al-ghalaba" (overcoming) here there are two opinions. The first: by subjugation and domination, if it is said that the verse is specific. (p-374)

The second: by the manifestation of proof, if it is said that the verse is general.

Regarding ﴿and wretched is the resting place﴾ there are two opinions. The first: "Wretched is what they have prepared for themselves," said by Mujahid.

The second: its meaning is "wretched is the abode," said by al-Hasan.

Regarding "bi'sa" (wretched) there are two views. The first: it is derived from "ba's" (might/severity), meaning intensity.

The second: it is derived from "ba'sa" (adversity), meaning evil.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿There has already been for you a sign in the two groups which met: one group fighting in the way of Allah﴾ — meaning the believers from among the people of Badr.

﴿And another, disbelieving﴾ — meaning the polytheists of the Quraysh.

﴿They saw them as twice their number by sight of the eye﴾. Regarding "mithlayhim" (twice them) there are two opinions. The first: they were two additional equivalents beyond the established number, so the number became three times, said by al-Farra'.

The second: it refers to an increase in what was seen, said by al-Zajjaj.

They differed about the addressee of this seeing, according to two opinions. The first: it is the believing group who fight in the way of Allah, in that Allah showed them the polytheists of the Quraysh on the Day of Badr as twice their own number, because the number of the Muslims was three hundred and some odd ten men, while the number of the polytheists, according to the narration of ʿAli and Ibn Masʿud, was a thousand; and according to the narration of ʿUrwa, Qatadah, and al-Rabiʿ, it was between nine hundred and a thousand. So Allah made them appear few in their eyes to strengthen their souls. This was said by Ibn Masʿud and al-Hasan.

The second: the group which Allah showed this to is the disbelieving group; Allah showed them the Muslims as twice their number, magnifying them, so that their hearts would be weakened thereby.

The verse concerning the two groups is about making the many appear few in the eyes of the Muslims, and making the few appear many in the eyes of the polytheists. And what preceded of the promise of victory came true, through killing, capture, and taking of captives. (p-375)

﴿And Allah supports with His help whom He wills﴾ — meaning from among the people of His obedience.

Regarding "ta'yid" (support) there are two opinions. The first: it is assistance. The second: it is strength.

﴿Indeed, in that is a lesson for those of vision﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: that in Allah's support of His Messenger on the Day of Badr, despite the fewness of his companions, is a lesson for those possessing insight and intellect. The second: that in what the polytheists saw of the large number of the Muslims despite their fewness is a lesson for those possessing eyes and insight.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 14–15:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾. The meaning of "zuyyina" (beautified) is: the love of desires was made appealing (ḥussina). Desire (al-shahwah) is among the creations of God in man, because it is a necessity that one cannot prevent.

Regarding the one who beautifies the love of desires, there are three opinions. The first: it is Satan, because no one is more blameworthy of it than God, Who created it. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: the interpretation that God beautified the love of desires by what He placed in natures of contention, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 7]. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: God beautified from the love of them what is good, and Satan beautified from the love of them what is ugly. (p-376)

﴿And the heaped-up piles of gold and silver (al-qanatir al-muqantarah)﴾. They differed regarding the measure of the qintar (qintar, a unit of weight) in seven opinions. The first: it is one thousand and two hundred ounces (ūqiyyah). This is the saying of Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Abu Hurayrah, and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred ounces." The second: it is one thousand and two hundred dinars. This is the saying of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥasan narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ. The third: it is twelve thousand dirhams or one thousand dinars. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is eighty thousand dirhams, or a hundred ratl of gold. This is the saying of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatadah.

The fifth: it is seventy thousand. This was said by Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid.

The sixth: it is the filling of a bull's hide with gold. This was said by Abu Nadrah.

The seventh: it is abundant wealth. This is the saying of al-Rabi'.

Regarding "al-muqantarah" (heaped-up) there are five opinions. The first: it means multiplied. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: it means complete and gathered together.

The third: it means nine qanatir. This was said by al-Farra'.

The fourth: it means minted into dirhams or dinars. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

The fifth: it means made into that form, as in their saying: "dirhams mudarhamah" (coins made into dirhams).

The second: al-musawwamah means the beautiful ones. This was said by Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, and al-Suddi.

The third: they are the trained ones. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The fourth: they are those prepared for jihad. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

The fifth: it derives from al-sima (the mark), with the word being both maqsur and mamdud. This was said by al-Ḥasan, and the poet said:

A youth whom God has blessed with beauty in his youth, having a mark that does not offend the eye.

﴿And the livestock (al-an'am)﴾ are the camels, the cattle, and the sheep and goats from the sheep and the goats. The word "al-na'am" is not said of any one kind of them alone except for camels specifically.

(And the tilth (al-harth)) is the crops.

It may also bear a second sense: that it means the land of tillage, because it is the origin, and al-harth would then mean the tilled thing (al-mahrūth).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 14–15:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Beautified for people is the love of desires﴾. The meaning of "zuyyina" (beautified) is: the love of desires was made appealing (ḥussina). Desire (al-shahwah) is among the creations of God in man, because it is a necessity that one cannot prevent.

Regarding the one who beautifies the love of desires, there are three opinions. The first: it is Satan, because no one is more blameworthy of it than God, Who created it. This was said by al-Ḥasan.

The second: the interpretation that God beautified the love of desires by what He placed in natures of contention, as He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have made what is on the earth an adornment for it﴾ [al-Kahf: 7]. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: God beautified from the love of them what is good, and Satan beautified from the love of them what is ugly. (p-376)

﴿And the heaped-up piles of gold and silver (al-qanatir al-muqantarah)﴾. They differed regarding the measure of the qintar (qintar, a unit of weight) in seven opinions. The first: it is one thousand and two hundred ounces (ūqiyyah). This is the saying of Mu'adh ibn Jabal and Abu Hurayrah, and Zirr ibn Ḥubaysh narrated it from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: The Messenger of God ﷺ said: "The qintar is one thousand and two hundred ounces." The second: it is one thousand and two hundred dinars. This is the saying of al-Ḍaḥḥāk and al-Ḥasan, and al-Ḥasan narrated it from the Prophet ﷺ. The third: it is twelve thousand dirhams or one thousand dinars. This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: it is eighty thousand dirhams, or a hundred ratl of gold. This is the saying of Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Qatadah.

The fifth: it is seventy thousand. This was said by Ibn 'Umar and Mujahid.

The sixth: it is the filling of a bull's hide with gold. This was said by Abu Nadrah.

The seventh: it is abundant wealth. This is the saying of al-Rabi'.

Regarding "al-muqantarah" (heaped-up) there are five opinions. The first: it means multiplied. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The second: it means complete and gathered together.

The third: it means nine qanatir. This was said by al-Farra'.

The fourth: it means minted into dirhams or dinars. This is the saying of al-Suddi.

﴿And the livestock (al-an'am)﴾ are the camels, the cattle, and the sheep and goats from the sheep and the goats. The word "al-na'am" is not said of any one kind of them alone except for camels specifically.

(And the tilth (al-harth)) is the crops.

It may also bear a second sense: that it means the land of tillage, because it is the origin, and al-harth would then mean the tilled thing (al-mahrūth).

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿the patient (al-sabirin)﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations (ta'wilat). The first: the patient in refraining from the sins they were forbidden.

The second: meaning in calamities. (p-378)

The third: the fasting ones.

It may also bear a fourth: those who are patient in refraining from the love of desires that has been made attractive to people.

﴿And the truthful (al-sadiqin)﴾. Regarding it there are two aspects. The first: in their speech.

The second: in speech, action and intention. Truthfulness in speech is informing with the truth; truthfulness in action is completing the deed; and truthfulness in intention is carrying out one's resolve.

﴿And the obedient (al-qanitin)﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: meaning those who obey, as said by Qatadah.

The second: its meaning is those who stand in worship, as said by al-Zajjaj.

﴿And the spenders (al-munfiqin)﴾. Regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: in jihad.

The second: in all acts of righteousness.

﴿And those who seek forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours (al-mustaghfirin bil-asḥar)﴾. Regarding it there are three interpretations. The first: meaning those who pray at the pre-dawn hours, as said by Qatadah.

The second: that they are those who verbally seek forgiveness at the pre-dawn hours, asking God Most High for forgiveness, as said by Ibn Umar, Ibn Mas'ud and Anas ibn Malik.

The third: that they attend the dawn prayer in congregation, as said by Zayd ibn Aslam.

Al-sahar (the pre-dawn) from the night is the period just before dawn.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 18–20:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Allah bears witness that there is no god but He﴾. Regarding this witness from Allah there are three opinions. The first: it means "Allah has decreed that there is no god but He." The second: it means "Allah has made clear that there is no god but He." The third: it is the testimony from Allah that there is no god but He.

It may carry two meanings. The first: that its meaning is an informing of this, as an affirmation of the report through direct witnessing, like a witness informing of what he has seen, because that is the more emphatic form of report. The second: that He brought into being, through His acts, a witnessing which stands in the place of testimony that there is no god but He. As for the testimony of the angels and those endowed with knowledge, it is their acknowledgement of what they have witnessed of the signs of His oneness.

﴿Standing in justice﴾, that is, with justice.

The standing of His justice may bear two senses. The first: that He undertakes justice on their behalf, from the saying of people, "So-and-so has taken up this matter" when he has undertaken it, so that standing means undertaking. The second: its meaning is that the standing of what He created and decreed in justice, that is its stability, so that His standing means permanence.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Indeed, the religion with Allah is Islam﴾. In this there are two senses. The first: the one who is religious with Allah through Islam is the one who is safe from the prohibitions. The second: that religion here means obedience, so it is as if He said: indeed, obedience to Allah is Islam.

Regarding the origin of the word Islam there are two opinions: (p-380)

The first: that its root is taken from al-salam (peace, safety), because it returns to safety. The second: that its root is submission (al-taslim) to the command of Allah in acting by His obedience.

﴿And those who were given the Scripture did not differ﴾. Concerning the People of the Book who differed, there are three opinions. The first: they are the People of the Torah from among the Jews, said by al-Rabi'. The second: they are the People of the Gospel from among the Christians, said by Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr. The third: they are the People of all the Scriptures, and "the Scripture" is meant as a genus without specification, which is the saying of some later scholars.

Regarding what they differed about there are three opinions. The first: about their religions after knowledge of their validity. The second: about Jesus and what they said about him of exaggeration and excess. The third: about the religion of Islam.

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿out of envy among themselves﴾, there are two senses. The first: their seeking leadership. The second: their deviation from the path of truth.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿And if they argue with you, say: I have submitted my face to Allah﴾, the verse.

In this there are two senses. The first: that is, I have submitted myself, and the meaning of "I have submitted" is that I have yielded to His command in sincerely making Him alone the One God. The second: that the meaning of "I have submitted my face" is: I have directed my intention sincerely to Allah in worship, taken from the saying of a man who, when he meets a man on the road, says: "This is my face toward you," meaning: this is my intention.

﴿And the unlettered ones﴾ are those who have no Scripture, taken from the unlettered (ummi) who does not write. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the polytheists of the Arabs.

﴿Have you submitted?﴾ is a command to Islam in the form of a question. (p-381)

If it is said: in His command, when they argue, that he should say "I have submitted my face to Allah," is there a turning away from answering them and a yielding to their argument? To this there are two answers. The first: His command to say this does not require forbidding answering them or yielding to their argument; rather His command is that he inform them of what his belief requires, and then he answers them and argues against them in accordance with what the question requires. The second: they did not argue with him seeking the truth, so answering them would not be obligatory; they argued only to display obstinacy, so it was permitted for him to turn away from them by what he was commanded to say to them.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 21–22:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve in the signs of Allah and kill the prophets without right and kill those who enjoin justice among the people﴾. Hamzah recited: (وَيُقاتِلُونَ الَّذِينَ يَأْمُرُونَ) (wa-yuqatilūna alladhīna ya'murūna, "and fight those who enjoin"). It was said that it is also so in the Codex of Ibn Mas'ud.

Regarding (al-qist) here, there are two views. The first: justice (al-'adl).

The second: enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil (al-amr bi'l-ma'ruf wa'l-nahy 'an al-munkar).

﴿So give them tidings of a painful punishment﴾. It is narrated from Abu 'Ubaydah ibn al-Jarrah, who said: "I said: O Messenger of Allah, who among the people will have the most severe punishment on the Day of Resurrection? He said: A man who kills a prophet, or a man who enjoins good or forbids evil. Then he recited this verse. Then he said: (O Abu 'Ubaydah, the Children of Israel killed forty-three prophets at the beginning of the day in a single hour. Then a hundred men and twelve men from the worshippers of the Children of Israel stood up and enjoined good upon those who had killed them and forbade them from evil, and they were all killed at the end of that same day)." (p-382)

(Fa-bashshirhum) means "so inform them." The usual sense of bushra (glad tidings) is information of good, though it may be used for information of evil, as it is used in this place. As for the reason for this naming, there are two views. The first: because it changes the complexion of the face, with joy in good news and with grief in bad news. The second: because it is news by which the skin is made to receive (an effect).

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 23–25:

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿Have you not considered those who were given a portion of the Scripture?﴾ That is, a share (ḥazẓ), because they knew some of what it contains.

﴿They are called to the Book of Allah﴾ Regarding the Book to which they were called, there are two opinions. The first: it is the Torah, to which the Jews were called, but they refused. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is the Qur'an, because what it contains agrees with what is in the Torah regarding the fundamentals of the religion. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that it may judge between them﴾, there are three opinions. The first: the prophethood of the Prophet ﷺ. The second: the matter of Ibrahim (Abraham), and that his religion is Islam. The third: that it is one of the prescribed punishments (ḥudud).

﴿Then a faction of them turns away, while they are refusing⦆ Ibn ʿAbbas said: this faction of those who turned away were the leaders of the Jews of Banu Qaynuqa: al-Nuʿman ibn Awfa and Bahri ibn ʿAmr ibn Suriya. They turned away from him concerning the punishment for adultery when he informed them that it is stoning, and he stoned the two Jewish adulterers.

If it is said: turning away from something means refusing it, it is answered: its meaning is that they turn away from the one who calls them and refuse what they are called to.

His saying, may He be exalted and glorified: ﴿They say: The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days.﴾ This is a statement of the Jews, and they differed regarding these days, with three opinions. The first: they are the days in which they worshipped the calf, which were forty days. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ.

The second: they are seven days. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The third: they are intermittent, as the punishment ends within them. This is the view of some of the later scholars.

﴿And what they used to fabricate has deluded them in their religion﴾ Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it is their saying: "We are the sons of Allah and His beloved ones." This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: it is their saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." This is the view of Mujahid.

The first: they are the days in which they worshipped the calf, which were forty days. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ.

The second: it is their saying: "The Fire will not touch us except for a few numbered days." This is the view of Mujahid.

(p-٣٨٤)

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿Say: "O Allah, Owner of sovereignty﴾. There are three interpretations of this:

The first: he means the sovereignty of the affairs of this world and the Hereafter.

The second: the Owner of the servants and of what they possess. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The third: the Owner of prophethood. This was said by Mujahid.

﴿You give sovereignty to whom You will, and You take sovereignty away from whom You will﴾. There are three interpretations of this. The first: that sovereignty here means prophethood. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: that it means faith.

The third: that it means authority (sultan).

Qatada narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) asked his Lord to grant the kingdom of Persia and Byzantium to his community, so Allah revealed this verse.

﴿And You honour whom You will, and You abase whom You will﴾. This may carry three meanings. The first: You honour whom You will through obedience, and You abase whom You will through disobedience.

The second: You honour whom You will through victory, and You abase whom You will through subjugation.

The third: You honour whom You will through wealth, and You abase whom You will through poverty.

﴿In Your hand is the good﴾, meaning: You are capable of it. He singled out good for mention, although He is capable of both good and evil, because it is good that is desired in its doing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿You make the night enter into the day, and You make the day enter into the night﴾. There are two views on this. The first: its meaning is that You cause the lessening of the night to enter into the increase of the day, and the lessening of the day into the increase of the night. This is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun).

The second: that its meaning is that You make the night a replacement for the day, and the day a replacement for the night. This is the view of some later scholars.

﴿You bring the living out of the dead, and You bring the dead out of the living﴾. Nafi', Hamza and al-Kisa'i read (al-mayyit) with tashdid (gemination of the yā', i.e. the doubled letter). The rest read it with takhfif (the single, undoubled form). (p-٣٨٥)

They differed about its meaning in the takhfif and tashdid forms. The Kufans held that al-mayt (with takhfif) is the one who has died, and al-mayyit (with tashdid) is the one who has not yet died.

Abu al-Abbas related from the scholars of Basra as a whole that the two are the same. He recited the verse of Ibn al-Ra'la' al-Qilabi:

"He who has died and found rest is not a dead man;
the dead man is the dead among the living.
The dead man is he who lives in misery,
his affairs overcast, with little hope."

Regarding the interpretation of bringing the living out of the dead, there are two views. The first: that He brings the living animal out of the dead drop (nutfah), and brings the dead drop out of the living animal. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Mujahid, Qatada and al-Suddi.

The second: that He brings the believer out of the disbeliever, and brings the disbeliever out of the believer. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Qatada said: Allah named Yahya ibn Zakariyya "Yahya" only because Allah, Mighty and Majestic, gave him life (ahyahu) through faith.

﴿And You provide for whom You will without reckoning﴾. Regarding this there are three sayings, which have already passed.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 28–34:

His saying, may He be exalted and majestic: ﴿Indeed, Allah chose Adam and Noah and the family of Abraham and the family of ʿImran over the worlds﴾. Regarding "the family of ʿImran" there are two opinions. The first: it refers to Moses and Aaron, the two sons of ʿImran.

The second: it refers to the Messiah, because Mary was the daughter of ʿImran. This is the opinion of al-Hasan.

Regarding the means by which He chose them, there are three opinions. The first: He chose them by choosing their religion for them. This is the opinion of al-Farra' (al-Farra', a grammarian and Qur'an scholar).

The second: He chose them by favouring them in the matters by which He distinguished them over the people of their times.

The third: He chose them by choosing them for prophethood. This is the opinion of al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, a grammarian and Qur'an scholar).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿offspring, one from another﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: they became offspring through mutual support, not through lineage, as He, may He be exalted, says: ﴿The hypocrite men and hypocrite women are one from another﴾ [al-Tawba: 67], meaning in their gathering upon misguidance. This is the opinion of al-Hasan and Qatada.

The second: they are offspring in terms of descent and lineage, since all of them are from the offspring of Adam, then from the offspring of Noah, then from the offspring of Abraham. This is the opinion of some of the later scholars.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 35–36:**

﴿When the wife of 'Imran said: "My Lord, I have vowed to You what is in my womb as one dedicated (to Your service). So accept it from me. Indeed, You are the Hearing, the Knowing."﴾ There are three opinions about it. The first is that *muharraran* (مُحَرَّرًا) means devoted solely to worship. This is the view of al-Sha'bi.

The second is that it means a servant of the *bay'ah* (بِيعَة, a Christian place of worship). This is the view of Mujahid.

The third is that it means freed from worldly affairs for the obedience of Allah. This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ja'far ibn al-Zubayr.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So when she delivered her, she said, "My Lord, I have delivered her as a female."﴾ She said this only as an apology for the departure from her vow, because the child was a female.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And Allah knows best what she delivered.﴾ Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr, on the authority of 'Asim, read *wada'at* (وَضَعَتْ) with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* (تَاءِ, the letter *tā'*). In that case, this is part of her apology, that Allah knows best what she delivered. The rest of the readers read it with a *jazm* (جَزْم, a sukūn) on the *tā'*. In that case, this is an answer from Allah, exalted is He, to her, that He knows best what she delivered of hers.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the male is not like the female.﴾ Because the female is not suited to what the male is suited to, namely serving the Holy Mosque, due to the menstruation that befalls her and to protecting women from *tabarruj* (تَبَرُّج, displaying their adornment before men). Such service is specific to boys.

﴿And I seek refuge for her in You and for her offspring from the accursed Satan.﴾ There are two interpretations of this. The first: its meaning is from the prodding of Satan, by which the newborn begins life crying out. Abu Hurayrah narrated this as a *marfū'* (مَرْفُوع, traced to the Prophet ﷺ). The second: its meaning is from his seduction of her. This is the view of al-Hasan. The meaning of *al-rajīm* (الرَّجِيم) is the one stoned with shooting stars.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 37:

His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He: ﴿So her Lord accepted her with a good acceptance﴾. Its meaning is that He was pleased with her in the vow she made, to devote herself to worship in Bayt al-Maqdis (the Holy House, Jerusalem).

﴿And He caused her to grow in a good growth﴾. He means: He brought her into being in a good way, in her nourishment and the goodness of her upbringing.

﴿And He entrusted her to Zakariyya﴾. The people of Kufa read (wa-kaffalaha) with the doubled letter (tashdid), and the meaning of that is that he handed over her guardianship (kafala) to someone else.

The rest read (kafalaha) without doubling (takhfif), and the meaning of that is that he took her guardianship upon himself.

﴿Every time Zakariyya entered upon her in the mihrab﴾. It is well known, and its origin is that it is the most honoured place in the assembly.

﴿He found with her provision﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: that the provision that came to her was summer fruit in winter and winter fruit in summer. This is the view of Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatada and al-Suddi.

The second: that she had never taken a breast at all until she spoke in the cradle, and that her provision used to come to her from Paradise. This is the view of al-Hasan.

They differed regarding the cause for which this provision came to her, on two views. The first: that it came to her by the supplication of Zakariyya for her. The second: that it came to her on account of the prophethood of the Messiah, peace be upon him.

﴿He said: O Mary, from where is this for you? She said: It is from Allah﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: that Allah, Exalted is He, was bringing her the provision. The second: that one of the righteous among His servants was subjected by Allah, Exalted is He, to her, as a kindness from Him toward her, so that her provision would come to her.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 42–44:

Allah's saying: ﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you over the women of the worlds."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: He chose her over the women of her time. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: He chose her for the bearing of the Messiah. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

(And purified you) Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: He purified you from disbelief. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: He purified you from the impurities of menstruation and postnatal bleeding. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

﴿And chosen you over the women of the worlds.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: it is an emphasis of the first choosing by repetition.

The second: the first choosing was for worship, and the second choosing was for the bearing of the Messiah.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord and prostrate and bow with those who bow.﴾ Concerning this there are three sayings. The first: it means, be sincere to your Lord. This is the saying of Sa'id.

The second: its meaning is, persist in obedience to your Lord. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The third: prolong standing in prayer. This is the saying of Mujahid.

﴿And bow with those who bow.﴾ Concerning the placing of prostration before bowing there are two opinions. The first: it was placed first in their law, although it is placed later according to us.

The second: the particle "waw" does not necessitate sequence, so the ruling of placing it first in wording and placing it later is equal. The original meaning of sujud is a strong lowering and humility, as the poet said:

"Both of them fell, and her head prostrated as a Christian woman prostrates without inclining."

Likewise ruku' (bowing) is similar, except that sujud is more lowering.

Concerning His saying Exalted is He: ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾ there are two opinions. The first: its meaning is, do as they do. The second: it means, with those who bow in congregational prayer.

Allah's saying: ﴿That is from the news of the unseen.﴾ It means what was of the good tidings of the Messiah.

﴿We reveal it to you.﴾ The original meaning of wahy (revelation) is the casting of meaning to its possessor. Revelation to the messengers is casting by sending down, to the bee by inspiration, and from one to another by gesture, as the Exalted said: ﴿So he revealed to them that they should glorify [Allah] in the morning and the evening.﴾ Al-Ajjaj said:

"... ... ... *** *** He revealed to it the settling, so it settled"

﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to determine] which of them would be responsible for Mary.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: they disputed over her and contended about her, seeking her guardianship. Zakariyya said: "I am most entitled to her, because her maternal aunt is with me." The people said: "We are most entitled to her, because she is the daughter of our imam and scholar." So they drew lots over her by casting their pens, which are arrows, facing the flow of the water. Zakariyya's staff faced the flow of the water rising upward, while their pens sank down, and Zakariyya won the lot. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and he took charge of her.﴾ This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, and al-Rabi'.

The second opinion: they pushed away her guardianship, because Zakariyya had already taken charge of her without drawing lots. Then a shortage of strength to bear her expenses came upon him, so he said to the people: "Let one of you take her." They pushed away her guardianship and refused it, so he cast lots between them and himself, and the lot fell to him. This is the saying of Sa'id.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 42–44:

Allah's saying: ﴿And when the angels said, "O Mary, indeed Allah has chosen you and purified you and chosen you over the women of the worlds."﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: He chose her over the women of her time. This is the saying of al-Hasan.

The second: He chose her for the bearing of the Messiah. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

(And purified you) Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: He purified you from disbelief. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

The second: He purified you from the impurities of menstruation and postnatal bleeding. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

﴿And chosen you over the women of the worlds.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: it is an emphasis of the first choosing by repetition.

The second: the first choosing was for worship, and the second choosing was for the bearing of the Messiah.

His saying, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿O Mary, be devoutly obedient to your Lord and prostrate and bow with those who bow.﴾ Concerning this there are three sayings. The first: it means, be sincere to your Lord. This is the saying of Sa'id.

The second: its meaning is, persist in obedience to your Lord. This is the saying of Qatadah.

The third: prolong standing in prayer. This is the saying of Mujahid.

﴿And bow with those who bow.﴾ Concerning the placing of prostration before bowing there are two opinions. The first: it was placed first in their law, although it is placed later according to us.

The second: the particle "waw" does not necessitate sequence, so the ruling of placing it first in wording and placing it later is equal. The original meaning of sujud is a strong lowering and humility, as the poet said:

"Both of them fell, and her head prostrated as a Christian woman prostrates without inclining."

Likewise ruku' (bowing) is similar, except that sujud is more lowering.

Concerning His saying Exalted is He: ﴿and bow with those who bow﴾ there are two opinions. The first: its meaning is, do as they do. The second: it means, with those who bow in congregational prayer.

Allah's saying: ﴿That is from the news of the unseen.﴾ It means what was of the good tidings of the Messiah.

﴿We reveal it to you.﴾ The original meaning of wahy (revelation) is the casting of meaning to its possessor. Revelation to the messengers is casting by sending down, to the bee by inspiration, and from one to another by gesture, as the Exalted said: ﴿So he revealed to them that they should glorify [Allah] in the morning and the evening.﴾ Al-Ajjaj said:

"... ... ... *** *** He revealed to it the settling, so it settled"

﴿And you were not with them when they cast their pens, [to determine] which of them would be responsible for Mary.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions. The first: they disputed over her and contended about her, seeking her guardianship. Zakariyya said: "I am most entitled to her, because her maternal aunt is with me." The people said: "We are most entitled to her, because she is the daughter of our imam and scholar." So they drew lots over her by casting their pens, which are arrows, facing the flow of the water. Zakariyya's staff faced the flow of the water rising upward, while their pens sank down, and Zakariyya won the lot. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿and he took charge of her.﴾ This is the saying of Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, al-Hasan, and al-Rabi'.

The second opinion: they pushed away her guardianship, because Zakariyya had already taken charge of her without drawing lots. Then a shortage of strength to bear her expenses came upon him, so he said to the people: "Let one of you take her." They pushed away her guardianship and refused it, so he cast lots between them and himself, and the lot fell to him. This is the saying of Sa'id.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 45–47:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When the angels said: "O Mary, indeed God gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, Jesus son of Mary"﴾. Regarding his being named "the Messiah" there are two opinions:

One: because he was anointed with blessing. This is the saying of al-Hasan and Sa'id.

The second: because he was anointed with purification from sins.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he will speak to the people in the cradle﴾. Regarding the reason for his speaking in the cradle there are two opinions:

One: to clear his mother of what she had been accused of.

The second: to manifest his miracle.

They differed: was he a prophet at the time of his speaking in the cradle? There are two opinions on this:

One: he was a prophet at that time, because of the manifestation of the miracle from him.

The second: he was not a prophet at that time, but God made that a foundation for his prophethood.

And al-Mahd (the cradle) is the lying place of the infant, derived from tamhid (spreading out/preparing).

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and in maturity﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions: One: that what is meant by al-kahl (maturity) is the forbearing (wise) one, and this is the saying of Mujahid.

The second: that he meant the kahl in age.

They differed on the age at which one attains kahl: [it is said to be] thirty-four years.

The second: that it is above the state of a youth and below the state of an old man, derived from strength, from their saying: "iktahala al-bayt" when it grew long and became strong.

If it is said: what is the meaning of the report that he speaks "in maturity," when that is not considered strange? There are two opinions on this: One: that he will speak to them in maturity by the revelation that comes to him from God, exalted is He.

The second: that he speaks as an infant in the cradle with the speech of one who is mature in age.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When Jesus perceived their disbelief, he said, "Who will be my helpers in (the cause of) God?"﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: it means, "Who will be my helpers with God?"

Second: its meaning is, "Who will be my helpers in the path to God?" This is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri).

Third: its meaning is, "Who will help me toward the help of God?"

The singular of al-Ansar (the helpers) is nasir (helper).

﴿The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said, "We are the helpers of God."﴾ There is disagreement about the reason they were named al-Hawariyyun (the disciples), with three opinions. First: they were so named because of the whiteness of their garments. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Second: they were launderers who whitened garments. This is the view of Ibn Abi Najih. Third: they were the chosen companions of the prophets, named so for the purity of their hearts. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The root of al-Hawari (الحَوارِيّ) is al-hawar, which means intense whiteness. From it comes al-hawari (الحَوارِيّ) applied to fine flour because of its intense whiteness, and al-hawar means the purity of the whiteness of the eye.

They differed concerning the reason the Messiah sought help from the disciples, with three opinions: First: he sought their help seeking protection from the disbelievers who wanted to kill him when he made his call manifest. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid. Second: he sought their help so that he could establish the proof and make the truth manifest. Third: to distinguish the believer who agrees from the disbeliever who opposes.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So write us down among the witnesses.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions: One: it means, "Join what is between us and them through sincerity in piety." Two: "Record our names with their names, so that we may obtain what they obtained of honor."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they schemed, and God schemed, and God is the best of schemers.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions: One: they schemed against the Messiah, peace be upon him, by devising a trick against him to kill him, and God's scheming was in turning them back in failure by casting the likeness of the Messiah upon another. This is the view of al-Suddi. Two: they schemed by concealing disbelief, and God's scheming was by requiting them with punishment. The phrase "and God schemed" was permitted for the sake of parallelism in speech, even though it departs from its strict sense, like His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], while the second act is not (in fact) a transgression. The root of al-makr (المَكْر) is al-iltifaf (enveloping, twisting together), and for this reason a thick intertwined tree is called makr. Al-makr is the devising of a plot against a person by enveloping him in what he dislikes.

The difference between al-makr (المَكْر) and al-hilah (الحِيلَة) is that al-hilah may be for displaying what is difficult without intent to harm, whereas al-makr is the pursuit of bringing about what is disliked upon the one targeted.

The phrase "and God schemed" was permitted for the sake of parallelism in speech, even though it departs from its strict sense, like His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194], while the second act is not (in fact) a transgression. The root of al-makr (المَكْر) is al-iltifaf (enveloping, twisting together), and for this reason a thick intertwined tree is called makr. Al-makr is the devising of a plot against a person by enveloping him in what he dislikes.

The difference between al-makr (المَكْر) and al-hilah (الحِيلَة) is that al-hilah may be for displaying what is difficult without intent to harm, whereas al-makr is the pursuit of bringing about what is disliked upon the one targeted.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When Jesus perceived their disbelief, he said, "Who will be my helpers in (the cause of) God?"﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions:

First: it means, "Who will be my helpers with God?"

Second: its meaning is, "Who will be my helpers in the path to God?" This is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri).

Third: its meaning is, "Who will help me toward the help of God?"

The singular of al-Ansar (the helpers) is nasir (helper).

﴿The disciples (al-Hawariyyun) said, "We are the helpers of God."﴾ There is disagreement about the reason they were named al-Hawariyyun (the disciples), with three opinions. First: they were so named because of the whiteness of their garments. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Second: they were launderers who whitened garments. This is the view of Ibn Abi Najih. Third: they were the chosen companions of the prophets, named so for the purity of their hearts. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Dahhak.

The root of al-Hawari (الحَوارِيّ) is al-hawar, which means intense whiteness. From it comes al-hawari (الحَوارِيّ) applied to fine flour because of its intense whiteness, and al-hawar means the purity of the whiteness of the eye.

They differed concerning the reason the Messiah sought help from the disciples, with three opinions: First: he sought their help seeking protection from the disbelievers who wanted to kill him when he made his call manifest. This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid. Second: he sought their help so that he could establish the proof and make the truth manifest. Third: to distinguish the believer who agrees from the disbeliever who opposes.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So write us down among the witnesses.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions: One: it means, "Join what is between us and them through sincerity in piety." Two: "Record our names with their names, so that we may obtain what they obtained of honor."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 3, verses 55–58:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When God said, "O Jesus, I will cause you to die and raise you up to Me"﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions:

The first: its meaning is, "I will seize you by raising you to the heaven, without death through dying." This is the view of al-Hasan, Ibn Jurayj, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: "I will cause you to die a sleep-death for the raising to the heaven." This is the view of al-Rabi'.

The third: "I will cause you to die a death by dying." This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The fourth: that it is of the inversion (*al-muqaddam wa al-mu'akhkhar*, transposition of words in the sentence), with the meaning: "I will raise you, and cause you to die after that." This is the view of al-Farra'.

Concerning His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and raise you up to Me﴾, there are two opinions:

One: "I will raise you up to the heaven."

The second: its meaning is "I will raise you up to My honour."

﴿And purify you from those who disbelieve﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: that His purifying him from them is their being prevented from killing him.

The second: that it is His removing him from among them.

﴿And I will make those who follow you superior to those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection﴾. Concerning this there are two interpretations:

One: that they are above them in proof and argument.

The second: that they are above them in might and dominance.

Concerning who is meant by this, there are two opinions: (p-398)

One: that those who believed in him are above those who denied him and lied about him. This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, al-Rabi', and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: that the Christians are above the Jews, because the Christians are mightier and the Jews more humbled. In this there is evidence that there will not be a kingdom (*mamlaka*) of them until the Day of Resurrection, unlike the Romans.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, come to a word that is equitable between us and you"﴾ — the verse — and regarding the intended referents of this, there are two opinions. One: they are the Christians of Najran. This is the view of al-Hasan, al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: they are the Jews of Madinah. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Rabi', and Ibn Jurayj.

﴿And not take one another as lords instead of Allah﴾ — regarding this there are two interpretations. One: it is the obedience of followers to their leaders in their commands that involve disobedience to Allah. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

The second: it is the prostration of some of them to others. This is the view of Ikrimah.

**The Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on Surah 3, Verses 65–68**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O People of the Scripture, why do you argue about Abraham, when the Torah and the Gospel were not revealed until after him?﴾ The occasion of revelation of this verse was that "the Jews and the Christians gathered before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and disputed about him. The Jews said, 'He was nothing but a Jew,' and the Christians said, 'He was nothing but a Christian.' So this verse was revealed, refuting both groups by what it clarified of the revelation of the Torah and the Gospel after him."

» Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Here you are, arguing about what you have knowledge of.﴾ That is, what they found in their books.

﴿Why then do you argue about what you have no knowledge of?﴾ That is, concerning the matter of Abraham.

﴿And Allah knows, while you do not know.﴾ That is, the matter of Abraham.

﴿And you do not know.﴾ So seek it from its causes.

(p. 401)

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you disbelieve in the signs of God while you bear witness?﴾ There are three interpretations (ta'wil, the explanation of the intended meaning). The first: "while you bear witness" means you bear witness to what indicates its truth from your own Book, in which there is good news of it. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Rabi', and al-Suddi.

The second: "while you bear witness" means you bear witness to its like from the signs of the prophets, which you acknowledge.

The third: "while you bear witness" means you bear witness to what the proof has been established against you.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿O People of the Book, why do you confuse the truth with falsehood﴾. There are two interpretations: One of them is the distortion of the Torah and the Gospel. This is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd.

The second is calling people to show Islam at the beginning of the day and to turn back from it at its end, intending to create doubt among people about it. This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Qatadah.

The third is believing in Moses and Jesus while disbelieving in Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿And conceal the truth﴾ means what they found with them of the description of Muhammad (ﷺ) and the good news of him in their books, out of obstinacy on the part of their scholars.

﴿While you know﴾ means the truth, through what you have recognised from your books.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not believe except in one who follows your religion﴾. There are two views on this. One is that it means: do not affirm (as true) except for one who follows your religion.

The second is: do not acknowledge the truth except for one who follows your religion.

The interpretation of this has been disputed in two views. One is that they are all the Jews, who said this to one another. This is the view of al-Suddi and Ibn Zayd.

The second is that they are the Jews of Khaybar, who said this to the Jews of Medina. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The reason for their being forbidden to believe except in one who follows their religion has also been disputed in two views. One is that they were forbidden this lest it become a path for idol-worshippers to affirm him. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The second is that they were forbidden this lest they acknowledge him and then be obliged to act according to his religion, since they had acknowledged its validity.

﴿Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, [and] that anyone should be given the like of what you were given﴾. There are two views on this. One is that the sentence contains an omission, and its estimate is: "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, that no one should be given the like of what you were given, O Muslims." Then the negative particle (lā, "not") was omitted from the sentence, because of the implication of the discourse (dalīl al-khiṭāb, the meaning understood from the context) upon it, like His words: ﴿God makes clear to you that you should not go astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 176], meaning: do not go astray. This is the meaning of the view of al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj.

The second is that the meaning of the sentence is: "Say: Indeed, guidance is the guidance of God, so do not deny that anyone should be given the like of what you were given."

﴿Or they will argue with you before your Lord﴾. There are two views on this. One is that it means: "And do not believe that they will argue with you before your Lord, because they have no proof." This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second is that its meaning is: "until they argue with you before your Lord," in the sense of remote possibility, as one says: "You will not meet him until the Hour comes." This is the view of al-Kisa'i and al-Farra'.

Regarding His words, Exalted is He: ﴿He specially chooses for His mercy whomever He wills﴾. There are two views on this. One is that it is prophethood. This is the view of al-Hasan, Mujahid, and al-Rabi'.

The second is the Qur'an and Islam. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

They have disputed whether prophethood is a reward for deeds, in two views. One is that it is a reward owed by entitlement.

The second is that it is an act of grace (tafaddul), because He said: ﴿He specially chooses for His mercy whomever He wills﴾.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 3, verses 75–76:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the People of the Scripture is one who, if you entrust him with a qintar (a large measure of wealth), will return it to you﴾. The scholars differed over the entry of the particle بِ (*bi*, "with") before القِنْطار (*qintar*) and الدِّينار (*dinar*, a gold coin), on two views. The first: it entered to attach the trust to the amount, as it entered in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and let them circumambulate the Ancient House﴾ [al-Hajj: 29]. (p-403)

The second: it has the meaning of عَلى (*ʿala*, "over"), and its sense is: "And among the People of the Scripture is one who, if you entrust him over a qintar."

﴿except so long as you remain standing over him﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: except so long as you remain standing over him in demanding and collecting, and this is the view of Qatadah and Mujahid. The second: by constant insistence. The third: standing over his head, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿That is because they say, "There is no blame upon us concerning the unlettered (al-ummiyyin)."﴾ It means: concerning the wealth of the Arabs. Regarding the reason for their considering it permissible to take it, there are two views. The first: because they are polytheists from among non-People of the Scripture, and this is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi. The second: because they have departed from their religion under which we had dealt with them, and this is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Juraij. Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that he said: When this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Allah has belied the enemies of Allah. There is nothing from the time of ignorance except that it is under my feet, except trust, for it is to be returned to the righteous and the wicked."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 77:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who sell the covenant of Allah and their oaths for a small price﴾. Regarding the "covenant" (ʿahd) there are two views. The first: it is what Allah, may He be exalted, has made obligatory upon the human being of obedience to Him and of refraining from His disobedience. (p-404)

The second: it is what is in human reason of restraint from falsehood and submission to the truth.

﴿Those will have no share (khalāq) in the Hereafter.﴾ Regarding the original meaning of khalāq there are two views. The first: its origin is from khalq, with the kha' open, meaning "self" (nafs), and the sense of the sentence is: they have no portion.

The second: its origin is khuluq, with the kha' pronounced with a damma, because it is a portion of what noble character (khuluq karīm) necessitates.

﴿And Allah will not speak to them﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: Allah will not speak to them with what would gladden them, but He will speak to them with what would distress them at the time of reckoning, because He says: ﴿Then indeed upon Us is their reckoning﴾. The second: He will not speak to them at all, but He will refer their reckoning to the angels.

﴿And He will not look at them on the Day of Resurrection﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: He will not see them. The second: He will not bestow favour upon them.

﴿And He will not purify them﴾, that is, He will not judge them to be purified.

The scholars of tafsir differed regarding the occasion of revelation of this verse, in three statements. The first: it was revealed concerning a group of Jewish rabbis: Abu Rafiʿ, Kinana ibn Abi al-Huqayq, Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, and Huyayy ibn Akhtab, who wrote a book with their own hands, then swore that it was from Allah, concerning what they claimed, that there is no blame upon them regarding the gentiles (ummiyyin). This is the view of al-Hasan and ʿIkrima.

The second: it was revealed concerning al-Ashʿath and an opponent of his who disputed over a piece of land. The opponent stood up to take the oath, and this verse was revealed, so al-Ashʿath refrained and acknowledged the truth. (p-405)

The third: it was revealed concerning a man who swore a false oath to sell his goods at an inflated price. This is the view of ʿAmir and Mujahid.

The Qur'anic verse: ﴿It is not for a human being that Allah should give him the Scripture, judgment, and prophethood, and then he should say to the people, "Be servants to me rather than to Allah."﴾

The occasion of its revelation, as narrated by Ibn Abbas: "Some of the Jews said to the Prophet (ﷺ), 'Do you call us to worship you, as the Messiah called the Christians?' So this verse was revealed."

﴿But rather, be rabbaniyyin (those devoted to the Lord)﴾. On this there are three interpretations:

First: they are jurists and scholars. This is the view of Mujahid.

Second: they are wise and pious. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

Third: they are the rulers who manage the affairs of the people. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Regarding the root meaning of rabbani, there are two opinions. The first is that it is one who manages the affairs of people through his administration. This is the view of the poet:

"I was a man whose affairs you took up, and before you, those who managed me were lost, and the managers perished."

So the scholar is called rabbani because through knowledge he manages affairs.

The second is that it is derived from ʿilm al-Rabb (the knowledge of the Lord), which is the knowledge of religion. Thus the possessor of the knowledge that the Lord commanded is called rabbani.

The second is that it is derived from ʿilm al-Rabb (the knowledge of the Lord), which is the knowledge of religion. Thus the possessor of the knowledge that the Lord commanded is called rabbani.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 81–82:

Allah's words: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of the Prophets: "Whatever I give you of Scripture and wisdom..."﴾. Regarding the covenant (al-mithaq) there are two opinions. The first is that He took the covenant of the Prophets that they would take [this pledge] from their peoples, to affirm Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of ʿAli, Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatadah, and al-Suddi.

The second is that He took their covenant that they would believe in the Last Day (al-Akhirah). This is the view of Tawus.

﴿Then there came to you a Messenger﴾, meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿Confirming what is with you﴾, meaning from the Torah and the Gospel.

﴿You shall believe in him and you shall support him.﴾ He said: ﴿"Do you affirm and accept My burden (iṣr) upon that?"﴾ Al-Iṣr means the covenant (ʿahd), and regarding it there are two interpretations. The first: its meaning is, "You accepted My covenant upon that."

The second: "You took My covenant from those who follow you."

﴿They said, "We affirm it." He said, "Then bear witness,"﴾ meaning against your nations concerning this.

﴿And I am with you among the witnesses﴾, against you and against them. (p-407)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 83–85:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to Him has submitted whoever is in the heavens and the earth, willingly or by compulsion﴾. Regarding this there are six opinions:

The first: that the believer submits willingly, and the disbeliever submits by compulsion at the time of death. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: that it is the acknowledgment of servitude, even if among them are those who associate partners in worship. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: that it is the prostration of the believer willingly, and the prostration of the disbeliever's shadow by compulsion. This is also narrated from Mujahid.

The fourth: willingly, through desire for reward; and by compulsion, through fear of the sword. This is the view of Mattar.

The fifth: that the submission of the unwilling is when the covenant was taken from them, so they acknowledged it. This is the view of Ibn Abbas.

The sixth: its meaning is that they submitted through yielding and humility. This is the view of Amir al-Sha'bi and al-Zajjaj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 86–91:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve after their belief and then increase in disbelief - their repentance will never be accepted﴾. Concerning this there are four interpretations (ta'wilat):

The first: They are the Jews who disbelieved in the Messiah, then increased in disbelief by [disbelieving in] Muhammad (ﷺ); their repentance will not be accepted at the time of their death. This is the opinion of Qatadah.

The second: They are the People of the Book; their repentance will not be accepted for sins they committed while persisting in their disbelief. This is the opinion of Abu al-'Aliyah.

The third: They are a people who apostatized, then resolved to display repentance by way of equivocation (tawriyah), so Allah informed His Prophet of their inner state. This is the opinion of Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: They are the Jews and Christians who disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) after having believed in him before his mission (ba'th), then increased in disbelief until the arrival of their appointed terms (ajal). This is the opinion of al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 92:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾. Regarding al-birr (righteousness) there are three interpretations. The first: al-birr is the reward of Allah, the Exalted.

The second: it is the doing of good through which reward is deserved. (p-409)

The third: al-birr is Paradise, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

Regarding the words of the Exalted: ﴿until you spend﴾ there are three opinions. The first: it refers to the obligatory charities (al-sadaqat al-mafrudat), and this is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: it refers to all charities, obligatory and voluntary, and this is the view of Ibn Umar.

The third: it refers to every kind of good in the way of Allah, whether charity or otherwise.

Amr ibn Dinar narrated that he said: "When this verse was revealed, ﴿You will never attain righteousness until you spend from what you love﴾, Zayd ibn Harithah came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with a horse of his called (Sabal) and said: 'Give this in charity, O Messenger of Allah.' So he gave it to his son Usama. He said: 'O Messenger of Allah, I only wanted to give it in charity.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: '(Your charity has been accepted).'"

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 93–95:

﴿All food was lawful to the Children of Israel, except what Israel had made unlawful for himself﴾. The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the Jews denied the Prophet's (ﷺ) permission of eating camel meat. So God Most High informed them of its lawfulness for them, at the time when Israel had made it unlawful for himself. This is because when he was afflicted with the pain of the vein called ischias (ʿirq al-nasa), he vowed to make the veins unlawful for himself, and camel meat was among the most beloved foods to him.

They differed over whether Israel's prohibition on himself was by the permission of God Most High or not, and this is based on their disagreement over the ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) of the prophets, on two views. The first: it was only by His permission, and this is the view of those who claim that a prophet may not exercise ijtihad. (p-410)

The second: it was by his own ijtihad without permission, and this is the view of those who claim that the Prophet may exercise ijtihad.

They also differed over the Jews' prohibiting that for themselves, on two views. The first: they prohibited it for themselves, following Israel.

The second: the Torah was revealed with its prohibition, so they prohibited it after its revelation. The first is more sound.
