Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 96–97:

﴿Indeed, the first House established for mankind is that at Bakkah, blessed and a guidance for the worlds﴾. There is no disagreement among the people of tafsir (exegesis) that it is the first house established for worship. They differ only over whether it was the first house established for anything other than worship, and there are two views. The first is that many houses existed before it, and this is the view of al-Hasan. The second is that no house was established before it, and this is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

Regarding "Bakkah," there are three opinions. The first is that Bakkah is the Masjid (the mosque) and Makkah is the whole Haram (sacred precinct), and this is the view of Ibn Shihab and Damrah ibn Rabi'ah. The second is that Bakkah is Makkah, and this is the view of Abu 'Ubaydah. The third is that Bakkah is the place of the House, while Makkah is other than that, in the sense of the town (al-qaryah), and this is related from Malik.

Regarding the derivation of Bakkah, there are two views. The first is that it is derived from crowding (al-zahmah). It is said: "Tabakka al-qawm ba'duhum ba'dan" when they crowd one another, so Bakkah is the place where people crowd for the circumambulation (tawaf). The second view is that it was named Bakkah because it "breaks the necks" (tabukku a'naq) of the tyrants: whoever commits deviation therein with injustice is not left unpunished. (p. 411)

Regarding His words ﴿blessed﴾, there are two interpretations. The first is that its blessing is the reward that is deserved for intending to go to it. The second is that it is a sanctuary for whoever enters it, even for wild animals, so that the game and the hound gather together in it.

﴿In it are clear signs: the Station of Ibrahim﴾. Is the sign in the Station of Ibrahim the trace of his two feet, and it is a solid stone? And the signs other than the Station are: the safety of the one who fears, the awe of the House and its preventing anyone from overpowering it, the swift punishment of whoever transgresses therein, and what occurred in the pre-Islamic era concerning the People of the Elephant.

﴿And whoever enters it shall be safe﴾. Its meaning is that He inclined the hearts of the Arabs toward it in the pre-Islamic era, so that the offender, when he entered it, was safe.

As for in Islam, there are two views concerning it. The first is that it is safety from the Fire, and this is the view of Yahya ibn Ja'dah. The second is safety from fighting, by prohibiting al-ījāl (...) upon those who enter it. As for the prescribed punishments (hudud), they are carried out upon whoever commits an offence within it.

The scholars differed concerning the offender who enters it, regarding the enforcement of the legal punishment (hadd) upon him within it, and there are two views. The first is that it is enforced upon him, and this is the position of al-Shafi'i. The second is that it is not enforced until he is compelled to leave it, and this is the position of Abu Hanifah.

﴿And due to Allah from the people is the pilgrimage (hajj) to the House, for whoever is able to make his way to it﴾. Concerning "ability" (al-istita'ah), there are three opinions. The first is that it is by wealth, namely provision and a mount, and this is the view of al-Shafi'i. The second is that it is by the body, and this is the view of Malik. The third is that it is by wealth and body, and this is the view of Abu Hanifah.

﴿And whoever disbelieves, then indeed Allah is free from need of the worlds﴾. Concerning this there are three interpretations. The first: it means whoever disbelieves in the obligation of the hajj, by not regarding it as obligatory, and this is the view of Ibn 'Abbas. The second: he does not consider its performance to be righteousness nor its abandonment to be sinful, and this is the view of Zayd ibn Aslam. (p. 412)

The third: they are the Jews, because when the verse ﴿And whoever seeks other than Islam as a religion, it will never be accepted from him﴾ was revealed, they said, "We are Muslims," so they were commanded to perform the hajj but did not perform it, and so Allah revealed this verse.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 98–99:

﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, why do you avert [people] from the way of Allah those who have believed, seeking to make it crooked"﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: their averting them from the way of what they had been upon was the inciting of enmity between the Aws and the Khazraj, so that they would recall the wars of the Jahiliyyah (the Age of Ignorance) and separate. This was specifically an act of the Jews, and it is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is their denial of the Prophet (ﷺ) and their rejection of the confirmation of his description in their books. This was an act of both the Jews and the Christians, and it is the view of al-Hasan.

﴿Seeking to make it crooked﴾, i.e., you seek crookedness. It is with a kasra on the ʿayn ('iwaj), meaning deviation from the paths of truth, whereas ʿawaj with a fatha means a slant standing upright in a wall or a spear.

﴿And you are witnesses﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: it means "those of understanding" (ʿuqalaʾ), like His saying, ﴿Or he gives ear while he is a witness﴾ [Qaf: 37]. The second: it means witnesses to what was occurring of their averting from the way of Allah, and it was said: of their obstinacy and their lying.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 100–101:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ — meaning the Aws and the Khazraj.

﴿If you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture﴾ — meaning the Jews, in their inciting [of discord] among you.

﴿They will return you after your belief to disbelief﴾

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 100–101:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ — meaning the Aws and the Khazraj.

﴿If you obey a faction of those who were given the Scripture﴾ — meaning the Jews, in their inciting [of discord] among you.

﴿They will return you after your belief to disbelief﴾

﴿O you who believe, fear Allah with the fear that is due to Him﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions. The first: it means that He is obeyed and not disobeyed, thanked and not disbelieved in, and remembered and not forgotten. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

The second: it means guarding against all sins. This is the view of some of the mutasawwifun (Sufis).

The third: it means that they acknowledge the truth in both security and fear.

The fourth: it means that He is obeyed, and that no one other than Him is feared in abandoning obedience to Him.

They differed over whether it has been abrogated (naskh) into two views. One: it is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). This is the view of Ibn Abbas and Tawus.

The second: it has been abrogated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So fear Allah as much as you are able﴾ [at-Taghabun: 16]. This is the view of Qatadah, al-Rabi', al-Suddi, and Ibn Zayd.

﴿And hold fast, all together, to the rope of Allah﴾. Concerning this there are five interpretations. The first: the rope is the Book of Allah, the Exalted. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Qatadah, and al-Suddi. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "The Book of Allah is the rope of Allah extended from the heaven to the earth."

The second: it is the religion of Allah, which is Islam. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

The third: it is the covenant of Allah. This is the view of Ata.

The fourth: it is sincerity to Allah and monotheism. This is the view of Abu al-Aliyah.

The fifth: it is the community (al-jama'ah). This is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud.

It was called a rope because one who grips it is saved, just as one who holds onto a rope is saved from a well or something else.

﴿And do not become divided﴾. Concerning this there are two views. One: away from the religion of Allah, in which He commanded adherence to the community. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Qatadah.

The second: away from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

﴿And remember the favor of Allah upon you when you were enemies and He brought your hearts together﴾. Concerning who was meant by this verse there are two views. One: they are the polytheists of the Arabs, because of the conflicts that existed between them. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: they are the Aws and the Khazraj, because of the wars that existed between them in the Jahiliyyah, which continued for one hundred and twenty years, until Allah brought their hearts together through Islam, and those grudges were abandoned. This is the view of Ibn Ishaq.

**Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-'Uyun*) on Surah 3, verses 104–109:**

﴿On the day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾. He means by this the Day of Resurrection, because people on that day are divided between those rewarded with Paradise and those punished with the Fire. The face of the one rewarded is described as white because it is radiant with joy, and the face of the one punished is described as black because it is darkened with grief.

﴿As for those whose faces turn black: "Did you disbelieve after your faith? Taste the punishment for what you used to disbelieve."﴾ Regarding these people who disbelieved after their faith, there are four opinions:

The first: they are those who disbelieved after outwardly professing faith, by hypocrisy. This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: they are those who apostatized after their Islam. This is the view of Mujahid.

The third: they are those among the People of the Book who disbelieved in the Prophet (ﷺ) after having believed in him through his description and attributes. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

The fourth: they are all the disbelievers, because they turned away from what the acknowledgment of Tawhid requires, when Allah ta'ala made them testify against themselves: ﴿"Am I not your Lord?" They said, "Yes, we testify."﴾ [al-A'raf: 172]. This is the view of Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 110–112:

﴿You are the best nation brought forth for mankind﴾. If it is asked: why did He say "you were (kuntum) the best nation" and not "you are (antum) the best nation"? There are four answers to this.

The first: God, Exalted is He, had already given them the good news that they were the best nation, so He said "you were" (kuntum), referring to what had preceded in the good news. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

It has been related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "You complete seventy nations, you are the best of them and the most honored of them before God." The second: this is for emphasis of the matter, because what is past is taken as established, whereas what is immediately present is not yet past. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And God was ever Forgiving and Merciful﴾. The third: its meaning is that He created them as the best nation.

The fourth: "you were the best nation" in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz).

﴿They are not all alike: among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and a group with him embraced Islam, and the rabbis of the Jews said: "None believed in Muhammad except our worst people." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ up to His words: ﴿and they are among the righteous﴾.

﴿An upright community﴾ has three interpretations (taʾwilat, plural of taʾwil, interpretation). The first: "just," which is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj. The second: "standing in obedience to God," which is the view of al-Suddi. The third: "steadfast in the command of God, exalted is He," which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and al-Rabiʿ.

﴿They recite the signs of God in the hours of the night﴾. There are two interpretations regarding this: the first, "the hours of the night," which is the view of al-Hasan and al-Rabiʿ. The second, "the middle of the night," which is the view of al-Suddi.

Scholars differed about what is meant by the recitation at this time, on two views. The first: the ʿAtamah prayer (the night prayer, i.e., ʿIshaʾ), which is the view of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud. The second: the Maghrib and ʿIshaʾ prayers, which is the view of al-Thawri. (p-418)

﴿And they prostrate﴾. There are three interpretations: The first: it means the prostration of prayer. The second: it intends the prayer, because recitation does not occur in prostration or in bowing; this is the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Farraʾ. The third: its meaning is "they recite the signs of God in the hours of the night, and they are, along with that, prostrating."

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like the likeness of a wind in which is a freezing cold that strikes the tilth of a people who wronged themselves, and destroys it﴾. Scholars differed about its occasion of revelation on two views. The first: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan and his companions on the Day of Badr, when they backed one another against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The second: it was revealed concerning the spending of the hypocrites alongside the believers in fighting the polytheists, in a manner of hypocrisy.

The second: it means that they wronged themselves by sowing in a place unfit for sowing and at a time not suited to it, so a wind came and destroyed it. God, exalted is He, thus set this as a parable for the destruction of their spending.

﴿They are not all alike: among the People of the Book is an upright community﴾. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the occasion of its revelation (sabab al-nuzul) was that ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam and a group with him embraced Islam, and the rabbis of the Jews said: "None believed in Muhammad except our worst people." So God, exalted is He, revealed: ﴿They are not all alike﴾ up to His words: ﴿and they are among the righteous﴾.

﴿An upright community﴾ has three interpretations (taʾwilat, plural of taʾwil, interpretation). The first: "just," which is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Jurayj. The second: "standing in obedience to God," which is the view of al-Suddi. The third: "steadfast in the command of God, exalted is He," which is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, and al-Rabiʿ.

﴿They recite the signs of God in the hours of the night﴾. There are two interpretations regarding this: the first, "the hours of the night," which is the view of al-Hasan and al-Rabiʿ. The second, "the middle of the night," which is the view of al-Suddi.

Scholars differed about what is meant by the recitation at this time, on two views. The first: the ʿAtamah prayer (the night prayer, i.e., ʿIshaʾ), which is the view of ʿAbd Allah ibn Masʿud. The second: the Maghrib and ʿIshaʾ prayers, which is the view of al-Thawri. (p-418)

﴿And they prostrate﴾. There are three interpretations: The first: it means the prostration of prayer. The second: it intends the prayer, because recitation does not occur in prostration or in bowing; this is the view of al-Zajjaj and al-Farraʾ. The third: its meaning is "they recite the signs of God in the hours of the night, and they are, along with that, prostrating."

﴿The likeness of what they spend in this worldly life is like the likeness of a wind in which is a freezing cold that strikes the tilth of a people who wronged themselves, and destroys it﴾. Scholars differed about its occasion of revelation on two views. The first: it was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan and his companions on the Day of Badr, when they backed one another against the Messenger of God (ﷺ). The second: it was revealed concerning the spending of the hypocrites alongside the believers in fighting the polytheists, in a manner of hypocrisy.

O you who have believed, do not take as intimates (biṭānah) those other than your own, [for they will not spare you (ruin)].

It was said: It was revealed concerning a group of Muslims who had established close affection with some of the polytheists, Jews and hypocrites, because of companionship in the pre-Islamic period, so they were forbidden from that.

Biṭānah (the inner circle, confidants) are the particular people of a man who are privy to his affairs. The root is baṭn (belly, inside), and from it comes biṭānat al-thawb (the lining of a garment), because it lies against the body.

﴿They will not spare you any corruption﴾, meaning they do not fall short in regard to your affairs.

Khabāl means ruin and harm; its root meaning is corruption, and from it comes khabal (madness).

﴿They love that you suffer hardship﴾. Here there are two interpretations. One: they love your misguidance from your religion, and this is the statement of al-Suddi. The second: they love that you be put to difficulty (ta'annut) in your religion, meaning that they drive you toward hardship in it, and this is the statement of Ibn Jurayj. The root of ʿanat is hardship.

﴿Hatred has already appeared from their mouths﴾, meaning there has appeared from them what indicates it.

﴿And what their breasts conceal is greater﴾, than what has appeared.

﴿And [remember] when you went out in the morning from your family, assigning the believers their positions for battle.﴾ The scholars differed over the place in question, giving two opinions:

One is that it was the Day of Uhud. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Rabiʿ, Qatadah, al-Suddi, and Ibn Ishaq.

The second is that it was the Day of the Confederates (al-Ahzab). This is the view of al-Hasan and Mujahid.

( تُبَوِّئُ ) means: you take a dwelling in which you settle the believers (tubawwiʾu, "you settle/position").

The meaning of the verse is that you arrange the believers in their places.

﴿And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾ Concerning this there are three opinions:
First, He hears what the hypocrites say and knows what they conceal of threats.
Second, He hears what those who gave you counsel said, and knows what they conceal of sincere advice or deceit of hearts.
Third, He hears what the believers say and knows what they conceal of sincerity of intention.

﴿When two groups among you were about to lose heart﴾ On this there are two opinions. One is that they were the Banu Salamah and the Banu Harithah from the Ansar. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Jabir ibn ʿAbd Allah, al-Hasan, and Qatadah.

The second is that they were a people from the Muhajirun and the Ansar.

Regarding the cause of their intention to lose heart (al-fashal, "cowardice/faintheartedness"), there are two opinions:
One is that ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul called them to turn back from meeting the polytheists on the Day of Uhud. They were inclined to do so but did not act. This is the view of al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj.
The second is that they disagreed about going out in the morning or remaining (in Medina), until they were inclined toward cowardice. Al-fashal means cowardice.

﴿And Allah had already given you victory at Badr when you were weak.﴾ Badr is a water source where they stopped. It belonged to a man called Badr. Al-Zubayr ibn Bakkar said that he was Badr ibn al-Nadr ibn Kinanah, and the place was named after his companion. This is the view of al-Shaʿbi. Others said that rather, it is a name for it without being attributed to the name of any companion.

﴿And you were weak (adhillah)﴾ has two opinions:
One is weakness in resisting the enemy.
The second is paucity of numbers and weakness of condition.

Ibn ʿAbbas said: the Muhajirun on the Day of Badr were seventy-seven men, and the Ansar were two hundred and thirty-six men, while the polytheists numbered between nine hundred and a thousand.

[p-420]

﴿Remember when you said to the believers﴾: meaning, on the Day of Badr.

﴿Is it not sufficient for you that your Lord reinforce you with three thousand angels sent down?﴾ *Al-kifayah* is the amount that fills a need, and *al-iktifa'* is limiting oneself to it. *Al-imdad* is giving something in successive stages. The root meaning of *al-imdad* is increase, as in *madd al-ma'* (the rising of water), which is its increase.

﴿Yes, if you are patient and mindful of God, and they come upon you immediately, this very moment﴾: there are two interpretations of this. The first: "from this very direction," which is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: "from this very anger," which is the view of Mujahid, al-Dahhak and Abu Salih. The root of *al-faur* is the boiling of a cooking pot (*faur al-qidr*), its bubbling at the height of fever, and from it comes *faur al-ghadab* (the flare of anger), because it is like the boiling of a pot.

﴿Your Lord will reinforce you with five thousand angels, marked﴾: Ibn Kathir, 'Asim and Abu 'Amr read *musawwimin* with a kasra on the waw (*wa*), and its meaning is that they marked their horses with a sign. The rest read it with a fatha on the waw, *musawwamin*, and its meaning is that the horses were grazing freely, namely sent out to pasture. (p-422)

They differed about the marking (*al-taswim*) in two views. The first: it was with wool on the forelocks and ears of the horses. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Qatadah, Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

The second: the angels descended on the Day of Badr upon piebald horses, wearing yellow turbans. This is the view of Hisham ibn 'Urwah.

They differed about their number. al-Hasan said they were five thousand, and others said they were eight thousand.

Ibn 'Abbas said: the angels did not fight except on the Day of Badr.

﴿So that He may cut off a part of those who disbelieved﴾: there are two views on this. The first: it was on the Day of Badr, by killing their leaders and chiefs of disbelief. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

The second: it was on the Day of Uhud, when eighteen men were killed from among them. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿So that He may cut off a part﴾, and He did not say "a middle" (*wasat*), because *al-tarf* (the edge, part) is closer to the believers than the middle, so the cutting was specific to what was nearer to them, as God the Exalted says: ﴿those of the disbelievers who are near to you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 123], ﴿or He will humiliate them so that they return frustrated﴾. Regarding *yakbitahum* (humiliate them) there are two views: the first: it means to grieve them, which is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabi'. The second: *al-kabt* is to throw someone down on the face, which is the view of al-Khalil (Ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi).

The difference between *al-khaibah* (frustration) and *al-ya's* (despair) is that frustration only occurs after hope, whereas despair may occur before hope.

﴿You have no part in the affair﴾: there are three sayings on this. The first: you have no part in the affair regarding their punishment and their correction; that rests with God the Exalted, whether He accepts their repentance or punishes them.

The second: you have no part in the affair regarding what you wish and do concerning your companions and concerning them, and that rests with God the Exalted in what He does of kindness toward them in repentance and correction, or in punishment and retribution.

The third: it was revealed on an occasion when his front tooth (*rubā'iyatuhu*) was broken, ﷺ. They differed about the occasion in two views. The first: after his tooth was broken, some people said: "How can a people prosper who have done this to their Prophet, while he is eager for their guidance?" So this verse was revealed. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Anas ibn Malik, al-Hasan, Qatadah and al-Rabi'.

The second: the Prophet ﷺ then resolved to supplicate against them and sought permission for it, so this verse was revealed and he refrained. He was not permitted to do so because of what was known of the repentance of some of them.

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba﴾. He means by "consuming" (ta'kulu) "taking" (al-akhdh). Riba (usury, interest) is an increase in the amount owed in exchange for an extension of the term. This is the riba of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period), which was commonly practiced among them through deferral (nasi'ah).

﴿doubled and redoubled﴾. This means that when the term falls due, the creditor says to the debtor: "Either you pay, or you increase the debt (turbi)." If the debtor does not pay, the amount is doubled upon him. Then the same is done when the next term falls due, until it becomes "doubled and redoubled."

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾. This shows that riba is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir), for which the threat of the Fire is deserved.

The scholars differ regarding the Fire of the one who consumes riba, on two views. The first: it is like the Fire of the disbelievers, without distinction, holding to the apparent meaning. The second: it and the Fire of the sinners are lighter than the Fire of the disbelievers, because of the difference in the sins.

﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves﴾. As for "immorality" (fahishah) here, there are two views. The first: it refers to the major sins among the sins. The second: it refers to riba, and this is the view of Jabir and al-Suddi.

﴿or wrong themselves﴾. It has been said that this refers to the minor sins among the sins.

﴿remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: they remember Him in their hearts and do not forget Him, so that His remembrance helps them to repent and seek forgiveness. The second: they remember Allah verbally, by saying: "O Allah, forgive us our sins." Allah has made easy for this Ummah what He made severe for the Children of Israel, for when one of them committed a sin, it would be written at his door as the expiation of his sin: "Cut off your nose, cut off your ear," and the like. So seeking forgiveness was established instead. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

The third: it is remaining silent about the sin and not seeking forgiveness for it, and this is the view of al-Suddi. The fourth: it is the sin without repentance.

﴿O you who have believed, do not consume riba﴾. He means by "consuming" (ta'kulu) "taking" (al-akhdh). Riba (usury, interest) is an increase in the amount owed in exchange for an extension of the term. This is the riba of the Jahiliyyah (the pre-Islamic period), which was commonly practiced among them through deferral (nasi'ah).

﴿doubled and redoubled﴾. This means that when the term falls due, the creditor says to the debtor: "Either you pay, or you increase the debt (turbi)." If the debtor does not pay, the amount is doubled upon him. Then the same is done when the next term falls due, until it becomes "doubled and redoubled."

﴿And fear the Fire which has been prepared for the disbelievers﴾. This shows that riba is among the major sins (al-kaba'ir), for which the threat of the Fire is deserved.

The scholars differ regarding the Fire of the one who consumes riba, on two views. The first: it is like the Fire of the disbelievers, without distinction, holding to the apparent meaning. The second: it and the Fire of the sinners are lighter than the Fire of the disbelievers, because of the difference in the sins.

﴿And those who, when they commit an immorality or wrong themselves﴾. As for "immorality" (fahishah) here, there are two views. The first: it refers to the major sins among the sins. The second: it refers to riba, and this is the view of Jabir and al-Suddi.

﴿or wrong themselves﴾. It has been said that this refers to the minor sins among the sins.

﴿remember Allah and seek forgiveness for their sins﴾. Regarding this there are two views. The first: they remember Him in their hearts and do not forget Him, so that His remembrance helps them to repent and seek forgiveness. The second: they remember Allah verbally, by saying: "O Allah, forgive us our sins." Allah has made easy for this Ummah what He made severe for the Children of Israel, for when one of them committed a sin, it would be written at his door as the expiation of his sin: "Cut off your nose, cut off your ear," and the like. So seeking forgiveness was established instead. This is the view of Ibn Mas'ud and Ata' ibn Abi Rabah.

﴿And who forgives sins except Allah? And they do not persist in what they have done﴾. Regarding this there are four interpretations. The first: it refers to persistence (al-israr) in sins, and this is the view of Qatadah. The second: it is committing the sin once one intends it, and this is the view of al-Hasan. *and for every people there is a way and its leader.*

*Indeed, those of the Family of Hashim at al-Taff,*
*they emulated one another and set for the noble the practice of emulation.*

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 144–148:

﴿Muhammad is nothing but a messenger; messengers have passed away before him.﴾ The occasion of its revelation: when it was spread on the Day of Uhud that the Prophet (ﷺ) had been killed, some people said: "If he were a prophet, he would not have been killed." Others said: "Let us fight for the same cause for which he fought until we join him."

﴿So if he dies or is killed, will you turn back on your heels?﴾ Meaning: will you return to disbelief after your faith?

﴿And whoever desires the reward of this world, We will give him of it.﴾ On this there are three opinions: (p-428)

The first: whoever intends by his struggle the reward of this world, i.e., the spoils of war that he obtains. This is the view of some of the Basrans.

﴿And how many a prophet has fought, and with him many devoted servants (ribbiyyun)?﴾ Ibn Kathir, Nafi' and Abu 'Amr recited it as qatala (with the first verb read as "was killed"), while the rest read qatala (with "fought"). Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 149–153:

﴿And Allah had already fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission﴾. That is, you were killing them, according to all scholars. It is said: "Hassahu" (to destroy, to kill) means he killed him, because he was rendered powerless by His help.

﴿When you were climbing up and not turning aside for anyone﴾. The difference between al-ish'ad (ascending on level ground) and al-su'ud (ascending on a height) is that al-ish'ad is on level ground and al-su'ud is upward on a rise. This is the view of al-Farra', Abu al-Abbas, and al-Zajjaj. It is related from Ibn Abbas that they climbed up Mount Uhud in flight.

﴿While the Messenger was calling you from your rear﴾. It was said: he would say, "(O servants of Allah, return!)." This is related from Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi, and al-Rabi'.

﴿So He rewarded you with grief upon grief﴾. On this there are two views: (p-430)

One: grief upon grief (one sorrow following another).

The second: grief together with grief (sorrow accompanying sorrow).

Regarding the first grief and the second, there are two interpretations. One: the first grief was the killing and wounding, and the second grief was the rumor of the killing of the Prophet (ﷺ). This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabi'.

The second: grief on the Day of Uhud for the grief of the Day of Badr. This is the view of al-Hasan.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (*al-Nukat wa al-Uyun*) on surah 3, verses 154–155:

﴿Then He sent down upon you, after distress, security in the form of drowsiness overtaking a group of you, while another group was concerned only with themselves.﴾ The cause of this was that on the Day of Uhud the polytheists threatened the believers that they would return to fight them. Those among the believers whom the security overtook were ready for battle: they were Abu Talha, Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf, al-Zubayr ibn al-Awwam, and others. They slept until the security overtook them.

﴿And another group was concerned only with themselves﴾ out of fear. They were from among the hypocrites: Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul, Mu'attib ibn Qushayr, and those with them. Fear overtook them, so they did not sleep, because of their evil opinion.

﴿They think about Allah other than the truth, the thought of the Jahiliyyah﴾ meaning, in denying His promise.

﴿They say, "If we had any say in the matter, we would not have been killed here."﴾ Concerning this there are two views (p-٤٣١):

One: "We were brought out against our will, and had the decision been ours, we would not have gone out." This is the view of al-Hasan.

The second: meaning, "We have no share of victory, as we were promised," in a manner of denying that.

﴿Say: Even if you had been in your houses, those for whom killing was decreed would have gone forth to their resting places.﴾ Concerning this there are two views. One: meaning, had you stayed behind, those among you who were believers would have gone out, and they would not have stayed behind because of your staying behind.

The second: had you stayed behind, those for whom killing was decreed would still have gone out to their resting places, and their sitting would not have saved them.

﴿And that Allah might test what is in your breasts﴾ Concerning this there are two interpretations (ta'wil, meaning the figurative or intended sense of the text). One: that He would deal with you as one who is tested and examined.

The second: its meaning is that He would test the friends of Allah by what is in your breasts, and He attributed the testing to Himself to magnify His status.

﴿Indeed, those of you who turned away on the day the two hosts met﴾ Concerning them there are two interpretations. One: they are all of the polytheists who turned their backs at Uhud. This is the view of Umar, Qatada, and al-Rabi'.

The second: they are those who fled to Madinah at the time of the defeat. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿It was only Satan who caused them to slip because of some of what they had earned.﴾ Concerning this there are two views. One: it was their love of booty and their greed for life.

The second: Satan made them slip by reminding them of past sins they had committed, and they disliked being killed before sincerely repenting of them and leaving the wrongdoing connected with them. This is the view of al-Zajjaj.

﴿And Allah has certainly pardoned them.﴾ Concerning this there are two views. One: He was forbearing toward them, in that He did not hasten to punish them. This is the view of Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd.

The second: He forgave them their sin, to show that they had sincerely repented. (p-٤٣٢)

It is said that those who remained with the Prophet (ﷺ) did not flee; they were thirteen men. Among them were five of the Muhajirun: Abu Bakr, Ali, Talha, Abd al-Rahman, and Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas. The rest were from the Ansar.

﴿So by a mercy from Allah, you were gentle with them.﴾ That is, "by a mercy from Allah." The word *mā* here is a *ṣilah* (an extra particle, added for the beauty of the composition).

﴿What! When a calamity struck you, although you had inflicted twice as much (on the enemy), you said, "How is this?" (p-435)

Regarding ﴿it is from yourselves﴾ (min ʿindi anfusikum), there are three opinions as to what is "from themselves":

The first: their disagreement about going out of Madinah to fight on the Day of Uhud, although the Prophet ﷺ had ordered them to remain fortified within it. This is the view of Qatadah and al-Rabiʿ.

The second: their choosing ransom (fida') over killing for the seventy (captives) on the Day of Badr. It was said to them: "If you do that, from among you there will be killed the same number." This is the view of ʿAli and ʿUbaydah al-Salmani.

The third: the opposition of the archers on the Day of Uhud to the command of the Prophet ﷺ to remain at their post.

﴿And what struck you on the day the two hosts met was by the permission of Allah, and that He might know the believers﴾ Regarding this, there are two opinions: The first: that He might see the believers (i.e., make them manifest).

The second: that they might be distinguished from the hypocrites.

﴿And that He might know those who became hypocrites﴾ meaning ʿAbd Allah ibn Ubayy and his companions.

﴿And it was said to them, "Come, fight in the way of Allah"﴾ meaning: strive.

﴿or repel (the enemy)﴾ Regarding this, there are two opinions: The first: meaning increasing the numbers, even if they did not fight. This is the view of al-Suddi and Ibn Jurayj.

The second: its meaning is "stand guard with the horses if you do not fight." This is the view of Ibn ʿAwf al-Ansari.

﴿They said, "If we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you."﴾ It was said that ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn Haram said to them: [Fear Allah and do not abandon your Prophet. Then Ibn Ubayy said to him:] "Why should we kill ourselves? Turn back with us; if we knew there would be fighting, we would certainly follow you."

﴿They were, that day, nearer to disbelief than to faith﴾ because by displaying faith they were not judged by the rulings of the disbelievers; and they had been, before that, nearer to faith by displaying it. Then, by what they did, they became nearer to disbelief than to faith.

He said, "They say with their mouths," although speech can only be with the mouth, for two reasons: The first: emphasis.

The second: that speech is sometimes attributed metaphorically to one who is silent, when he is content with it.

And do not think of those who were killed in the way of Allah as dead; rather, they are alive. (Q. 3:169)

This means that they are in this state both at the time and after being killed. As for their condition in Paradise, it is known to all believers, and there is nothing impossible in their being brought to life in that way by divine wisdom.

Ibn Mas'ud, Jabir and Ibn 'Abbas narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When your brothers were struck at Uhud, Allah placed their souls in the crops of green birds that come to the rivers of Paradise and eat from its fruits."

Regarding ﴿alive with their Lord﴾ (Q. 3:169), there are two ta'wil (interpretations). The first is that they are in a state where no one can benefit or harm them except their Lord.

The second is that they are alive with their Lord in the sense that He knows they are alive, though people do not.

﴿And they rejoice in those who have not yet joined them from behind them﴾ (Q. 3:170). There are two views on this. The first is that they say: "Our brothers are being killed as we were, and they will receive from Allah's honour what we have received." This is the view of Qatadah and Ibn Juraij.

The second is that the martyr is brought a book containing the names of his brothers who will come to him, and he is given the good news of this, so he rejoices as the family of an absent person rejoices in the world at his return. This is the view of al-Suddi.

﴿Those to whom the people said: "Indeed, the people have gathered against you, so fear them"﴾ (Q. 3:173). As for "the people" in both places, although the word is in the plural form, it refers to a single person, since the meaning of the sentence is: the saying came from a certain person. Those to whom "the people" spoke were the Muslims. There are two views about the speaker of "the people":

The first is that he was a Bedouin to whom a reward was given for this, which is the view of al-Suddi.

The second is that he was Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud al-Ashja'i, which is the view of al-Waqidi.

The second "the people" were Abu Sufyan and his companions.

They differ over the time when Abu Sufyan intended to gather this force against them, on two views. The first is that it was after his return from Uhud in the third year (AH), until Allah cast terror into the hearts of the polytheists and they held back. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Ishaq and Qatadah.

The second is that it was at Badr al-Sughra in the fourth year (AH), a year after Uhud. This is the view of Mujahid.

The first is that he frightens the believers about his polytheist allies. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second is that he frightens his hypocrite allies so that they will hold back from fighting the polytheists. This is the view of al-Hasan and al-Suddi.

His Exalted saying: And let not those who withhold what Allah has given them of His bounty think that it is good for them; rather, it is bad for them (﴿وَلا يَحْسَبَنَّ الَّذِينَ يَبْخَلُونَ بِما آتاهُمُ اللَّهُ مِن فَضْلِهِ هو خَيْرًا لَهم بَلْ هو شَرٌّ لَهُمْ﴾). Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: they are those who withhold zakat, and this is the view of al-Suddi.

The second: they are the People of the Book who were stingy about clarifying to the people what is in their scriptures of the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Ibn Abbas, who said: "Did you not hear Him say: ﴿They are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon the people﴾?" That is, they conceal, and they command the people to concealment.

They will have the necks encircled with what they withheld on the Day of Resurrection (﴿سَيُطَوَّقُونَ ما بَخِلُوا بِهِ يَوْمَ القِيامَةِ﴾). Concerning it there are two opinions. The first: what they are encircled with is a bald venomous serpent (shuja' aqra'), and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud. The second: it is a collar of fire, and this is the view of Ibrahim.

And let not those who hasten to disbelief grieve you (﴿وَلا يَحْزُنْكَ الَّذِينَ يُسارِعُونَ في الكُفْرِ﴾). There are two opinions concerning them. The first is that they are the hypocrites (al-munafiqun), and this is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Ishaq.

The second is that they are a people among the Arabs who apostatized from Islam.

Indeed they will not harm Allah at all; Allah intends that He not give them a share in the Hereafter (﴿إنَّهم لَنْ يَضُرُّوا اللَّهَ شَيْئًا يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ ألا يَجْعَلَ لَهم حَظًّا في الآخِرَةِ﴾). Regarding His intention in this, there are three statements. The first: that He decrees it. The second: its meaning is that He will intend, in the Hereafter, to deprive them of their reward, because their faith has been nullified by their disbelief. The third: He intends to nullify their deeds on account of the sins they have deserved, and this is the view of Ibn Ishaq.

Allah would not leave the believers in the state you are in until He distinguishes the wicked from the good (﴿ما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيَذَرَ المُؤْمِنِينَ عَلى ما أنْتُمْ عَلَيْهِ حَتّى يَمِيزَ الخَبِيثَ مِنَ الطَّيِّبِ﴾). The good (al-tayyib) are the believers. The wicked (al-khabith) here has two interpretations. The first is the hypocrite, and this is the view of Mujahid. The second is the disbeliever, and this is the view of Qatadah and al-Suddi.

They differed regarding the means by which the distinguishing takes place, on two views. The first: by the imposition of jihad (taklif al-jihad), and this is the view of those who interpreted the wicked as the hypocrite. The second: by the proofs through which they are identified, and this is the view of those who interpreted it as the disbeliever.

Nor would Allah disclose to you the unseen (﴿وَما كانَ اللَّهُ لِيُطْلِعَكم عَلى الغَيْبِ﴾). It is said that the occasion of its revelation was that a group of the polytheists said: "If Muhammad is truthful, let him inform us who believes and who does not believe?" So this verse was revealed.

The first: what they are encircled with is a bald venomous serpent (shuja' aqra'), and this is the view of Ibn Mas'ud. The second: it is a collar of fire, and this is the view of Ibrahim.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿You will surely be tested in your wealth and your selves, and you will surely hear from those who were given the Scripture before you and from those who associated partners with Allah much harm.﴾ Concerning this harm there are three opinions:

The first: it is narrated that Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf used to satirize the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers and incite the polytheists against them, until Muhammad ibn Maslama killed him. This is the view of al-Zuhri.

The second: that Finhas the Jew, the chief of Banu Qaynuqa, when he was asked for a loan, said: "Your Lord has become needy, so that we must lend to Him." This is the view of Ikrimah.

The third: that the harm consisted of the shirk they heard, such as the saying of the Jews, "Uzayr is the son of Allah," and the saying of the Christians, "The Messiah is the son of Allah." This is the view of Ibn Jurayj.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 187–189:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when Allah took the covenant of those who were given the Book﴾. The mithaq (covenant) is an oath.

Regarding "those who were given the Book" here, there are three opinions. The first: they are the Jews specifically. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi. (p-442)

The second: they are the Jews and the Christians.

The third: they are everyone who was given knowledge of some part of a Book, for their prophets had taken their covenant.

﴿You shall surely make it clear to the people and not conceal it﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions. The first: that they should make clear the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Saʿid ibn Jubayr and al-Suddi.

The second: that they should make clear the Book in which his mention is found. This is the view of al-Hasan and Qatadah.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do not think that those who rejoice in what they have brought, and love to be praised for what they did not do﴾. Regarding "them" there are two opinions. The first: they are the People of the Book, who rejoiced at their unity in denying the Prophet (ﷺ) and concealing his matter, and loved to be praised for what was not in them, namely that they were people of devotion and knowledge. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Dahhak.

The second: they are the People of Hypocrisy, who rejoiced at their staying behind from fighting and loved to be praised for what was not in them of faith in Muhammad (ﷺ). This is the view of Abu Saʿid al-Khudri and Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 190–194:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we have heard a caller calling to faith, "Believe in your Lord," so we have believed﴾. Regarding the caller there are two opinions. The first: that it is the Qur'an, and this is the saying of Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: "Not everyone heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." (p-443)

The second: that it is the Prophet (ﷺ), and this is the saying of Ibn Jurayj and Ibn Zayd.

﴿Calling to faith﴾ means calling to faith (ila al-iman), like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿All praise is due to Allah, who guided us to this﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], meaning "to this."

And from it is the saying of the rajiz (a poet of the rajaz meter):

"He inspired it (al-qarar) so it settled, and held it fast with the firm, steadfast mountains."

He means: he inspired to it, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], meaning "to it."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. If it is said: they already knew that Allah, exalted is He, fulfills His promise, so what is the meaning of this supplication and request? There are four answers to this:

The first: that the purpose of it, while knowing that He fulfills His promise, is submission to Him through supplication and request.

The second: that this calls one to adhering to righteous deeds.

The third: its meaning is, "make us among those to whom You have promised Your reward."

The fourth: meaning, "hasten to us the fulfillment of Your promise and the bringing forward of Your victory."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, and grant us what You promised us through Your messengers﴾. If it is said: they already knew that Allah, exalted is He, fulfills His promise, so what is the meaning of this supplication and request? There are four answers to this:

The first: that the purpose of it, while knowing that He fulfills His promise, is submission to Him through supplication and request.

The second: that this calls one to adhering to righteous deeds.

The third: its meaning is, "make us among those to whom You have promised Your reward."

The fourth: meaning, "hasten to us the fulfillment of Your promise and the bringing forward of Your victory."

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verse 195:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So their Lord answered them: "Never will I allow to be lost the work of any worker among you, whether male or female"﴾. Mujahid and Amr ibn Dinar related that the occasion of the revelation of this verse was that Umm Salamah said: "O Messenger of Allah, why is it that men are mentioned in migration (hijrah) but not women?" So this verse was revealed.

﴿Some of you are from others﴾, meaning: females are from males, and males are from females.(p-444)

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 196–198:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you﴾. If it is said: the Prophet (ﷺ) is not susceptible to being deceived, so how was he addressed with this? There are two answers to this.

The first: Allah, mighty and majestic, said this to him only as discipline (ta'dib) and as a warning (tahdhir).

The second: it is an address to everyone who hears it, as if He had said: "Let not the going to and fro of those who disbelieve in the land deceive you, O listener."

Regarding their going to and fro there are two opinions. The first: it means their going to and fro in the comforts of the lands (fi na'im al-bilad).

The second: their going to and fro while not being seized for their sins.

Commentary of al-Mawardi (al-Nukat wa al-Uyun) on surah 3, verses 199–200:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And among the People of the Book are those who believe in God, and in what has been revealed to you, and in what has been revealed to them﴾. The scholars differed over the occasion of its revelation (asbab al-nuzul, the circumstances of revelation) in two views. The first: it was revealed concerning al-Najashi (the Negus). Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab narrated from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Go out and pray over a brother of yours." So he led us in prayer with four takbirs, and said: "This is al-Najashi, Ashama." The hypocrites said: "Look at this man praying over a Christian ilj (a foreigner or serf) whom he has never seen!" So God revealed this verse. This is the view of Qatada.

The second: it was revealed concerning 'Abd Allah ibn Salam and others among the Muslims of the People of the Book. This is the view of Mujahid and Ibn Jurayj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, be steadfast, outdo (others) in steadfastness, and stand ready (rabitu, guard the frontiers)﴾. Concerning it there are four interpretations:

The first: "Be steadfast in obedience to God, outdo the enemies of God in steadfastness, and stand ready in the way of God." This is the view of al-Hasan, Qatada, Ibn Jurayj and al-Dahhak.

The second: "Be steadfast in your religion, outdo the promise that He made to you, and stand ready against My enemy and your enemy." This is the view of Muhammad ibn Ka'b.

The third: "Be steadfast in jihad, outdo the enemy, and stand ready by constant presence at the frontier (ribat, garrison duty)." It is derived from rabt al-nafs (binding of the self), and from it the saying of people: "God bound (rabata) His heart with patience." This is the meaning of the view of Zayd ibn Aslam.

The fourth: "Stand ready for the prayers by awaiting them, one after another." Al-'Ala' ibn 'Abd al-Rahman narrated from his father, from Abu Hurayra, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "Shall I not direct you to that by which God erases sins and raises ranks?" They said: "Yes, O Messenger of God." He said: "Perfecting the ablution in difficult conditions, frequent steps to the mosques, and waiting for one prayer after another. That is ribat."

The surah of Al 'Imran ends.
